title: The Most Important Habit in Your Classroom is Easy to Overlook
author: Doug Lemov
summary: Doug Lemov argues that extraordinary moments of teaching depend on mundane systems, and that the most important routine in any classroom is following directions. He defines a positive habit as something done automatically without being told, and a routine as a habit shared by a group. To show it, he analyses a short video of kindergarten teacher Audrian McFarlane using what he calls the what-to-do cycle: give clear and concrete directions, be seen looking, narrate the positive, and make small non-invasive corrections quickly. When attention drifts after a silent cheer, she steps in with a countdown, an anonymous individual correction and calm thanks, and is teaching again by 42 seconds. Lemov concludes that this is an orderly classroom achieved by technique rather than shouting or scolding.
points: Lemov holds that extraordinary teaching moments are invisibly dependent on mundane systems, and that following directions is the foundation of them.
He defines the what-to-do cycle as clear directions, being seen looking, narrating the positive and making small non-invasive corrections.
Anonymous individual corrections let a teacher show she has noticed without putting a student on stage.
Narrating the positive makes the norm of following through visible, and peer norms strongly shape behavior.
The kindergarten example shows a calm, early intervention restoring focus in about twenty seconds, with no scolding.
quotes: Extraordinary moments of teaching and learning are almost always “invisibly dependent” on more mundane systems that set the stage for them.
And the single most important routine in any classroom is one you might overlook: following directions.
If students are in the habit of doing what their teacher asks, everyone is focused, learning time is maximized, and disruptions are limited and easily resolved.
Acknowledgement is better than praise. But your goal is to make the “norm” of direction following visible to others.
Make small non-invasive corrections as soon as a student is slow to follow. Correct anonymously when possible.
She’s making the normalcy of following through on directions more obvious to students because what they perceive the peer norm to be will influence their behavior.
An orderly classroom, achieved with technique not shouting or scolding.
